data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms as a methodological rule of 'critical preference' rather than an inductive inference; it survives by redefining rational action as the selection of the theory that has withstood the most severe attempts at falsification, accepting the cost that this preference offers no guarantee of future success or increased probability of truth.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent requires a logical guarantee that the preferred theory will succeed in the next instance, the Popperian defense fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'preference' is defined strictly as assigning a higher subjective probability of truth, the defense collapses into the induction Popper rejected.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the context demands a justification for why nature should remain uniform based on past tests, the non-inductive stance cannot provide it.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'inductive justification' (claiming past success predicts future truth) and 'methodological selection' (choosing the best-tested available option for critical discussion and action). By treating corroboration as a report of past performance without probabilistic implications, the agent can prefer Theory A over Theory B because A has survived stricter tests, not because A is more likely to be true. This resolves the tension by framing action as a convention adopted to facilitate further testing and avoid known errors, rather than a bet on truth.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
